sentences.text: Carcharodontosaurus saharicus was a massive theropod that reached approximately 12 meters in length and weighed between 5 and 7 metric tons.
Its body plan featured a robust build with small forelimbs, an elongated tail, and a short neck.
The animal possessed uniquely thin, blade-like teeth that were distinct among its allosauroid relatives.
The complete neotype skull would measure 1.6 meters, a size comparable to the largest skulls of Tyrannosaurus.
A 2022 paper estimated the anterior bite force at 11,312 newtons and the posterior bite force at 25,449 newtons.
The genus was first described in 1925 by Charles Depéret and Justin Savornin based on two lost fossil teeth unearthed in 1924 from wall cuts near Timimoun in French Algeria.
French paleontologist René Lavocat first suggested the presence of the animal in the Lower Douira Formation in 1954 based on fragmentary fossils.
In 2025, the main specimen, which had previously been considered the holotype of Carcharodontosaurus, was redescribed as the holotype of a distinct genus named Tameryraptor.
The species had a high tooth replacement rate, allowing damaged teeth to be replaced easily, unlike extant bone-crushing mammals.
The lower bite force compared to Tyrannosaurus implies that it likely did not eat bones.

Spinosaurus and Suchomimus experienced greater skull stress than Carcharodontosaurus, suggesting they could only consume light, small prey, whereas Carcharodontosaurus could bite larger items while sustaining stress.
Isotopic analyses suggest Carcharodontosaurus was more terrestrial than the contemporary Spinosaurus, which pursued semi-aquatic habits.
The neotype skull preserves pathologies including signs of biting, infection, and breaks.
A later study identified an unusual bony projection on the nasal as a potential bite mark.
Daniel Chure suggested that the bony shelf above the orbit was used for head-butting fights.
Carcharodontosaurus is the type genus of the family Carcharodontosauridae and the subfamily Carcharodontosaurinae.
The clade Carcharodontosauridae was originally created by Stromer for Carcharodontosaurus and Bahariasaurus, but the name was not used until the late 20th century.
Carcharodontosaurus lived in Northwest Africa between 100 and 94 million years ago during the Cenomanian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
Carcharodontosaurians have been found from the Late Jurassic to the Mid-Cretaceous on every continent except Antarctica.
The subfamily Carcharodontosaurinae, containing Carcharodontosaurus, was likely restricted to the southern continent of Gondwana, where it probably served as an apex predator.
Many fossils from French expeditions in North Africa were assigned to Carcharodontosaurus based on limited information, though many now belong to other genera.
A 2016 study suggested that non-holotypic material assigned to C. iguidensis actually belongs to Sigilmassasaurus and an unrelated taxon, limiting the species to its holotype.
The Spanish tooth assigned to Carcharodontosaurus lacks typical carcharodontosaurid traits and resembles other allosauroids instead.
